title: Reading Practice 7 - The Psychology of Decision Making
description: IELTS Academic Reading practice about cognitive biases and how people make choices.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: The Psychology of Decision Making
stimuli.content:
A Every day, humans make thousands of decisions, ranging from trivial choices about what to eat to life-changing decisions about careers and relationships. For centuries, economists and philosophers assumed that people make decisions rationally, carefully weighing costs and benefits to maximise their utility. However, research in cognitive psychology and behavioural economics over the past fifty years has revealed that human decision-making is far from rational, being systematically influenced by cognitive biases and mental shortcuts known as heuristics.

B One of the most well-documented cognitive biases is the anchoring effect, first described by psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in 1974. This bias causes people to rely too heavily on the first piece of information they encounter when making decisions. In one classic experiment, participants were asked to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations after being shown a random number on a spinning wheel. Those who saw a higher number consistently gave higher estimates, even though the wheel was clearly random.

C Loss aversion is another powerful bias that affects decision-making. Research has consistently shown that people feel the pain of losing something about twice as strongly as they feel the pleasure of gaining something of equal value. This asymmetry leads to risk-averse behaviour in many situations and helps explain why people often stick with the status quo even when change would be beneficial. Loss aversion also influences consumer behaviour, as marketers have learned to frame offers in terms of what customers might lose rather than gain.

D Understanding cognitive biases has important practical implications. In medicine, doctors who are aware of confirmation bias can make more accurate diagnoses. In finance, investors who understand loss aversion can make better portfolio decisions. Governments around the world have established behavioural insights teams that use knowledge of cognitive biases to design better public policies.
